examples.derivation: For x≠2, multiplying by (x−2)² preserves the inequality: x−2>(x−2)², so (x−2)(x−3)<0. The upward-opening quadratic has roots 2 and 3 and is negative precisely between them. Thus 2<x<3; both endpoints are excluded. The plotted polynomial and labelled roots agree. This follows the squared-denominator and graphical interval methods taught at source lines 174–215.
For x≠3, multiplication gives (x+2)(x−3)≤2(x−3)². Their difference factors as (x−3)(x−8), which must be non-negative. Thus x<3 or x≥8 after exclusion. The upward quadratic and labelled roots agree.

For x≠2,-3, multiplying by (x-2)²(x+3)² gives (x-2)(x+3)[(x+3)-(x-2)]>0, hence 5(x-2)(x+3)>0. The upward quadratic is positive outside its roots, giving x<-3 or x>2. The plotted expression and intercepts agree.
For x≠0, multiplying by 9x² gives 9x>x³, hence x(x-3)(x+3)<0. Across roots -3,0,3, the signs are negative, positive, negative, positive. Thus x<-3 or 0<x<3. The plotted cubic agrees.

For x≠1, multiplying by (x-1)² gives 12(x-1)≤x(x-1)². Rearrangement yields (x-1)(x²-x-12)=(x-1)(x-4)(x+3)≥0. The non-negative intervals are [-3,1] and [4,∞); excluding 1 gives [-3,1)∪[4,∞). The plotted expression and intercepts agree.
